title: Products of Vectors and Scalars in Mechanics
short_intro: Vector algebra involves operations such as scalar (dot) and vector (cross) products that combine vector quantities in mechanics. These operations form the mathematical foundation for analyzing force, torque, angular momentum, and work.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Geometrical interpretation of dot and cross products, orthogonal unit vectors, work done by constant and variable forces, torque, and condition for perpendicularity and parallelism.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Scalar triple products (box product), vector triple products, applications to central forces, Coriolis acceleration, angular velocity vectors, and rotational mechanics.

prerequisites: Resolution of a vector into rectangular components in 3D Cartesian coordinates
Basic trigonometric identities and properties of determinants

concept_notes.heading: Scalar Product (Dot Product)
bullets: Defined as the product of the magnitudes of two vectors and the cosine of the smaller angle between them: A · B = AB cos(θ).
Results in a scalar quantity; commutative (A · B = B · A) and distributive over vector addition.
Orthogonal unit vectors satisfy i · i = j · j = k · k = 1 and i · j = j · k = k · i = 0.

concept_notes.heading: Vector Product (Cross Product)
bullets: Defined as a vector whose magnitude is AB sin(θ) and whose direction is given by the right-hand rule perpendicular to the plane containing A and B.
Non-commutative and anticommutative: A × B = -(B × A).
Orthogonal unit vectors satisfy i × i = 0, i × j = k, j × k = i, and k × i = j.

concept_notes.heading: Scalar Triple Product
bullets: Expressed as A · (B × C), representing the volume of the parallelepiped formed by vectors A, B, and C.
Cyclic permutation leaves the scalar triple product invariant: A · (B × C) = B · (C × A) = C · (A × B).
If the scalar triple product is zero, the three vectors are coplanar.

concept_notes.heading: Vector Triple Product
bullets: Expressed as A × (B × C), resulting in a vector lying in the plane of B and C.
Evaluated using the BAC-CAB rule: A × (B × C) = B(A · C) - C(A · B).
Essential in deriving the kinematics of rotational motion and central force trajectories.

derivations.title: Cartesian Component Expansion of Dot Product
derivations.conditions: Vectors given in terms of their orthogonal components in 3D space.
steps: Let A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k and B = B_x i + B_y j + B_z k.
Expand the dot product: A · B = (A_x i + A_y j + A_z k) · (B_x i + B_y j + B_z k).
Apply distributive property and orthogonality relations (i · i = 1, i · j = 0).
derivations.result: A · B = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z

derivations.title: Cartesian Component Expansion of Cross Product
derivations.conditions: Vectors given in terms of their orthogonal components in 3D space.
steps: Let A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k and B = B_x i + B_y j + B_z k.
Write the cross product as a determinant: A × B = det([[i, j, k], [A_x, A_y, A_z], [B_x, B_y, B_z]]).
Expand the determinant along the first row.
Substitute fundamental cross products of unit vectors.
derivations.result: A × B = (A_y B_z - A_z B_y)i - (A_x B_z - A_z B_x)j + (A_x B_y - A_y B_x)k

graphs_and_experiments.title: Geometric Projection in Dot Product
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two vectors A and B originating from the same point, with a perpendicular dropped from the tip of B onto vector A to show B cos(θ).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The dot product represents the product of the magnitude of one vector and the scalar projection of the second vector onto the first.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions regarding work done and components.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Parallelogram Area via Cross Product
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parallelogram formed by adjacent vectors A and B, highlighting the height h = B sin(θ).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The magnitude of the cross product |A × B| equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by A and B.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in calculating angular momentum and torque magnitudes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Right-Hand Screw Rule Verification
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A 3D coordinate system showing the rotation from vector A to vector B curling the fingers of the right hand, with the thumb pointing along A × B.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Determines the unambiguous direction of axial vectors like torque and angular velocity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Crucial for sign conventions in rotational dynamics and electromagnetism.

solved_numericals.question: Find the angle between the two vectors A = 3i + 4j + 5k and B = 3i + 4j - 5k.
solution_steps: Calculate the dot product: A · B = (3)(3) + (4)(4) + (5)(-5) = 9 + 16 - 25 = 0.
Use the dot product formula: A · B = AB cos(θ).
Since A · B = 0 and magnitudes are non-zero, cos(θ) = 0.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the torque of a force F = (2i - 3j + 4k) N acting at a position r = (3i + 2j + 3k) m about the origin.
solution_steps: Set up the cross product matrix for τ = r × F = det([[i, j, k], [3, 2, 3], [2, -3, 4]]).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the vectors A = i - j + k, B = 2i + j - k, and C = i + 2j + 2k.
solution_steps: The volume is given by the scalar triple product V = |A · (B × C)|.
Construct the determinant with rows as components of A, B, and C: det([[1, -1, 1], [2, 1, -1], [1, 2, 2]]).

assumptions_and_limitations: Vector products assume a three-dimensional Euclidean space with a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system.
Scalar and vector products are defined for spatial vectors; pseudo-vectors (axial vectors like torque) obey specific transformation rules under spatial inversion (parity).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The cross product of two vectors is another vector that depends on the choice of origin.
common_misconceptions.correct: The cross product of two free vectors is independent of the coordinate origin, though position-dependent vector products (like torque) do depend on the chosen pivot.
common_misconceptions.why: Cross products of displacement or force vectors independent of reference points are geometric entities.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A × B is equal to B × A.
common_misconceptions.correct: A × B = -(B × A) due to the anticommutative property of the vector product.
common_misconceptions.why: Reversing the order changes the direction of the right-hand rule thumb by 180 degrees.

quick_revision: Dot product yields a scalar (A B cos θ); cross product yields a vector (A B sin θ n-hat).
Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product; parallel vectors have zero cross product.
BAC-CAB rule: A × (B × C) = B(A · C) - C(A · B).
Scalar triple product vanishing implies coplanarity of three vectors.
